title: Ἕκτωρ ὑπὸ Ἀχιλλεῖ
titleEn: The Chase and the Challenge — Iliad 22.188–288
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Achilles still drives Hector round the walls, and keeps the Trojan archers from shooting so that the glory stays his. Zeus weighs the two fates in his golden scales, and Hector’s sinks, so that Apollo leaves him. Athena comes to Achilles and tells him to rest while she goes to persuade Hector to stand and fight. She takes the shape of his brother Deiphobus and tempts him out with a promise of help. Face to face with Achilles, Hector offers a bargain that whoever wins will give back the other’s body, and Achilles refuses it in the words of lions and men, wolves and lambs. Achilles throws first and misses, Athena returns his spear unseen, and Hector, with a taunt, throws his own.

sentences.t: Ἕκτορα δ’ ἀσπερχὲς κλονέων ἔφεπ’ ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς.
sentences.tr: Hektora d’ asperches kloneōn ephep’ ōkys Achilleus.
sentences.l: Hector unceasingly throwing into confusion pursued, swift Achilles.
sentences.i: Swift Achilles pursued Hector without pause, throwing him into confusion.
sentences.n: The word order puts the object first: Ἕκτορα ‘Hector’ is the object, and the subject, ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς ‘swift Achilles’, comes last, after the verb. κλονέων is the present participle of κλονέω, ‘throw into confusion’, and ἀσπερχές ‘without pause’ is an adverb. ἔφεπ’ is the unaugmented imperfect of ἐφέπω ‘pursue’, with its final vowel elided. ὠκύς ‘swift’ is a stock epithet and is translated every time. The part opens in the middle of the chase round Troy.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτε νεβρὸν ὄρεσφι κύων ἐλάφοιο δίηται
ὄρσας ἐξ εὐνῆς διά τ’ ἄγκεα καὶ διὰ βήσσας·
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hote nebron oresphi kyōn elaphoio diētai
orsas ex eunēs dia t’ ankea kai dia bēssas·
sentences.l:
And as when on the mountains a hound a deer’s fawn pursues,
having roused it from its lair, through the valleys and through the glens;
sentences.i: As when on the mountains a hound, having roused a deer’s fawn from its lair, chases it through valleys and through glens —
sentences.n: This is a comparison (ὡς δ’ ὅτε ‘and as when’), and it runs on into the next unit. The hound (κύων) is the subject, the fawn (νεβρόν) the object, and ἐλάφοιο is the genitive of ἔλαφος, so ‘a deer’s fawn’. δίηται is a subjunctive of δίεμαι ‘chase’ (the subjunctive after ὅτε is the usual mood of a general picture); ὄρσας is the aorist participle of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’. ὄρεσφι ‘on the mountains’ has the old ending -φι, which stands for a plain case; ἄγκεα ‘valleys’ and βήσσας ‘glens’ are the two kinds of country it is driven through.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ εἴ πέρ τε λάθῃσι καταπτήξας ὑπὸ θάμνῳ,
ἀλλά τ’ ἀνιχνεύων θέει ἔμπεδον ὄφρά κεν εὕρῃ·
sentences.tr:
ton d’ ei per te lathēisi kataptēxas hypo thamnōi,
alla t’ anichneuōn theei empedon ophra ken heurēi·
sentences.l:
and him, even if it escapes his notice, having cowered under a bush,
yet tracking it he runs steadily until he finds it;
sentences.i: and even if the fawn escapes the hound’s notice by cowering under a bush, the hound still runs on, tracking it steadily, until it finds it;
sentences.n: Read τόν as ‘him’, meaning the hound: λανθάνω ‘escape the notice of’ takes the accusative of the one who fails to notice, so ‘even if it escapes him’. The subject of λάθῃσι is the fawn, and καταπτήξας (aorist participle of καταπτήσσω ‘cower in fear’) belongs to it. The hound is the subject of θέει, ‘runs’, and of εὕρῃ, an aorist subjunctive with κεν after ὄφρα ‘until’. ἀνιχνεύων ‘tracking’ is a present participle; ἔμπεδον is ‘steadily’. The Greek names neither animal in this unit, and the free English supplies the nouns.

sentences.t: ὣς Ἕκτωρ οὐ λῆθε ποδώκεα Πηλεΐωνα.
sentences.tr: hōs Hektōr ou lēthe podōkea Pēleïōna.
sentences.l: So Hector did not escape the notice of the fleet-footed son of Peleus.
sentences.i: So Hector did not escape the notice of the fleet-footed son of Peleus.
sentences.n: ὥς ‘so’ applies the comparison. οὐ λῆθε is the unaugmented imperfect of λήθω (the poetic form of λανθάνω), with the accusative of the one who notices, exactly as in the unit before: Hector is the subject and Achilles the one who is not escaped. ποδώκεα ‘fleet-footed’ is the stock epithet (accusative singular in -εα, Attic -η) and Πηλεΐωνα ‘son of Peleus’ the patronymic that stands for Achilles; both are translated every time.

sentences.t:
ὁσσάκι δ’ ὁρμήσειε πυλάων Δαρδανιάων
ἀντίον ἀΐξασθαι ἐϋδμήτους ὑπὸ πύργους,
εἴ πως οἷ καθύπερθεν ἀλάλκοιεν βελέεσσι,
sentences.tr:
hossaki d’ hormēseie pylaōn Dardaniaōn
antion aïxasthai eÿdmētous hypo pyrgous,
ei pōs hoi kathyperthen alalkoien beleessi,
sentences.l:
And as often as he would rush for the Dardanian gates
to dart against them, beneath the well-built towers,
in case from above they might keep harm off him with shafts,
sentences.i: Every time he made a dash for the Dardanian gates, to dart at them beneath the well-built towers, in the hope that those above might keep harm off him with their shafts,
sentences.n: ὁσσάκι … τοσσάκι ‘as often as … so often’ is a pair: this unit holds the first half, the next the second. ὁρμήσειε is an optative of repeated action in the past (‘whenever he made a dash’), and ἀΐξασθαι ‘to dart’ is an infinitive of purpose. Δαρδανιάων is the epic genitive plural of ‘Dardanian’, naming the gates of Troy. ἀλάλκοιεν is an aorist optative of ἀλαλκεῖν ‘keep off’ with οἱ ‘for him’; the Greek does not say what is kept off, so ‘harm’ is supplied, and the men on the towers are the subject. βελέεσσι is the epic dative plural ‘with shafts’.

sentences.t:
τοσσάκι μιν προπάροιθεν ἀποστρέψασκε παραφθὰς
πρὸς πεδίον·
sentences.tr:
tossaki min proparoithen apostrepsaske paraphthas
pros pedion·
sentences.l:
so often in front of him he would turn him back, having got ahead,
toward the plain;
sentences.i: so often Achilles would get ahead of him and turn him back toward the plain;
sentences.n: τοσσάκι ‘so often’ answers ὁσσάκι. ἀποστρέψασκε carries the iterative suffix -σκ-, which makes a past tense mean ‘used to, would’: ‘he would turn back’, again and again. The subject is Achilles, though the Greek only says ‘he’; παραφθάς is the aorist participle of παραφθάνω ‘get ahead of’, and προπάροιθεν ‘in front’. πεδίον is the open plain, as against the city.

sentences.t: αὐτὸς δὲ ποτὶ πτόλιος πέτετ’ αἰεί.
sentences.tr: autos de poti ptolios petet’ aiei.
sentences.l: but he himself toward the city flew always.
sentences.i: while he himself kept always flying along on the side of the city.
sentences.n: αὐτὸς δέ ‘but he himself’ sets the subject against μιν ‘him’ in the last unit, so ‘he himself’ is still Achilles: he keeps to the city side and Hector is turned toward the plain. ποτί is the epic form of πρός and πτόλις of πόλις; the genitive after ποτί gives the sense ‘on the side of the city’. πέτετ’ is the present of πέτομαι ‘fly’, with its ending elided, and αἰεί is Attic ἀεί ‘always’.

sentences.t: ὡς δ’ ἐν ὀνείρῳ οὐ δύναται φεύγοντα διώκειν·
sentences.tr: hōs d’ en oneirōi ou dynatai pheugonta diōkein·
sentences.l: And as in a dream he is not able to pursue one fleeing;
sentences.i: And as in a dream one cannot pursue a man who is running away;
sentences.n: A second comparison, and a different kind of picture: a dream. The subject of δύναται ‘is able’ is left out (‘one’). ἐν ὀνείρῳ is the dative singular of ὄνειρος ‘dream’, φεύγοντα ‘one fleeing’ is the accusative participle of φεύγω, and διώκειν ‘to pursue’ is the infinitive.

sentences.t: οὔτ’ ἄρ’ ὃ τὸν δύναται ὑποφεύγειν οὔθ’ ὃ διώκειν·
sentences.tr: out’ ar’ ho ton dynatai hypopheugein outh’ ho diōkein·
sentences.l: neither then can this one flee from that, nor that one pursue;
sentences.i: neither can the one get away from the other, nor can the other pursue him;
sentences.n: Here ὁ and τόν are the article used as a pronoun, ‘this one’ and ‘that one’. The first ὁ is the one who flees: he cannot ὑποφεύγειν ‘flee from under’, that is, get clear of τόν, the pursuer. The second ὁ is the pursuer, who cannot διώκειν ‘pursue’; the verb has no object stated. οὔτε … οὔτε ‘neither … nor’, with οὔθ’ elided before the rough breathing of ὁ.

sentences.t: ὣς ὃ τὸν οὐ δύνατο μάρψαι ποσίν, οὐδ’ ὃς ἀλύξαι.
sentences.tr: hōs ho ton ou dynato marpsai posin, oud’ hos alyxai.
sentences.l: so this one could not seize that one with his feet, nor that one escape.
sentences.i: so Achilles could not catch Hector on foot, nor Hector get away from him.
sentences.n: The application of the dream-picture. ὃ τὸν … μάρψαι: ὁ ‘this one’ is Achilles, who could not μάρψαι ‘seize’ τόν ‘that one’, Hector; δύνατο is the unaugmented imperfect of δύναμαι. ποσίν ‘with his feet’ is the dative plural of πούς, and gives ‘on foot’. In οὐδ’ ὃς ἀλύξαι the ὅς is once more the article as a pronoun (‘that one’, Hector), not a relative; ἀλύξαι is the aorist infinitive of ἀλύσκω ‘escape’ and depends on δύνατο understood.

sentences.l:
And how would Hector have escaped from under the death-spirits of death,
if not for him, for the last and final time, Apollo had met
near at hand, who roused in him might and quick knees?
sentences.i: And how could Hector have escaped the spirits of death, if Apollo had not met him for the last and final time, close at hand, and roused might and quick knees in him?
sentences.n: A question that expects the answer ‘he could not’. κεν with the aorist ὑπεξέφυγεν (‘fled out from under’) and εἰ μή with the imperfect ἤντετ’ (ἀντάω ‘meet’, with οἱ ‘him’) make a condition that did not hold. κῆρας is the plural of κήρ, a death-spirit, one of the powers that bring death; the house wording ‘death-spirits of death’ is used every time. πύματον … ὕστατον ‘last and final’ is adverbial. In ὅς οἱ ἐπῶρσε the ὅς is a relative (‘who’); ἐπῶρσε is the aorist of ἐπόρνυμι ‘rouse in’, and μένος is ‘might’. γοῦνα is epic for γόνατα ‘knees’, and λαιψηρά is ‘quick’.

sentences.t:
λαοῖσιν δ’ ἀνένευε καρήατι δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς,
οὐδ’ ἔα ἱέμεναι ἐπὶ Ἕκτορι πικρὰ βέλεμνα,
μή τις κῦδος ἄροιτο βαλών, ὃ δὲ δεύτερος ἔλθοι.
sentences.tr:
laoisin d’ aneneue karēati dios Achilleus,
oud’ ea hiemenai epi Hektori pikra belemna,
mē tis kydos aroito balōn, ho de deuteros elthoi.
sentences.l:
To the troops signed a refusal with his head heavenly Achilles,
and did not allow them to let fly at Hector the bitter missiles,
lest someone win the glory by striking him, and he come second.
sentences.i: Heavenly Achilles made a sign of refusal to the troops with his head, and would not let them throw their bitter missiles at Hector, for fear that some man might win the glory by striking him, and he himself come second.
sentences.n: Achilles stops his own side from taking a shot. λαοῖσιν ‘to the troops’ is a dative plural, and ἀνένευε is the imperfect of ἀνανεύω ‘refuse by a sign’, whose house wording is ‘made a sign of refusal’; καρήατι is the epic dative of κάρη ‘head’. οὐδ’ ἔα is the imperfect of ἐάω ‘allow’, with ἱέμεναι ‘to let fly’; πικρά ‘bitter’ goes with βέλεμνα ‘missiles’. μή … ἄροιτο ‘lest … win’ is a fear-clause with the aorist optative of ἄρνυμαι ‘win, carry off’, and βαλών ‘by striking’ is the aorist participle of βάλλω. In ὃ δὲ δεύτερος ἔλθοι, ὁ is Achilles: ‘and he come second’. δῖος ‘heavenly’ is the stock epithet.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ τὸ τέταρτον ἐπὶ κρουνοὺς ἀφίκοντο,
καὶ τότε δὴ χρύσεια πατὴρ ἐτίταινε τάλαντα,
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē to tetarton epi krounous aphikonto,
kai tote dē chryseia patēr etitaine talanta,
sentences.l:
But when for the fourth time they came to the springs,
then indeed the father was holding out golden scales,
sentences.i: But when for the fourth time they reached the springs, then the Father held out his golden scales,
sentences.n: The laps are counted by the springs, the two springs of 22.147: this is the fourth time they reach them. τὸ τέταρτον is an adverbial accusative ‘for the fourth time’, and ἀφίκοντο the aorist of ἀφικνέομαι ‘arrive at’. πατήρ ‘the Father’ is Zeus, though the Greek does not name him here. ἐτίταινε is the imperfect of τιταίνω ‘stretch out’, and τάλαντα (our ‘talent’) are the scales, the balance. The second line repeats an earlier line of the poem word for word, with its English; the end is a comma here, because the sentence goes on.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ ἐτίθει δύο κῆρε τανηλεγέος θανάτοιο,
τὴν μὲν Ἀχιλλῆος, τὴν δ’ Ἕκτορος ἱπποδάμοιο,
sentences.tr:
en d’ etithei dyo kēre tanēlegeos thanatoio,
tēn men Achillēos, tēn d’ Hektoros hippodamoio,
sentences.l:
and in them he placed two death-spirits of death that lays-at-length,
the one of Achilles, the other of Hector, horse-taming,
sentences.i: and in them he put two spirits of death that lays men at length, one for Achilles and one for Hector, tamer of horses,
sentences.n: ἐν … ἐτίθει is tmesis, the preverb standing apart: ‘put in’, the objects going into the pans of the scales. κῆρε is the dual of κήρ ‘death-spirit’, and τανηλεγέος … θανάτοιο is ‘of death that lays at length’. The meaning of τανηλεγής is not known: ‘laying men out at full length’ (τανυ- ‘stretched’ + λέγω ‘lay’) is one reading, and ‘bringing long sorrow’ is another; the house wording takes the first. τὴν μὲν … τὴν δ’ ‘the one … the other’ divides the two. Ἀχιλλῆος is the epic genitive of Ἀχιλλεύς; ἱπποδάμοιο ‘horse-taming’ is the stock epithet of Hector, here in the genitive, and is translated every time.

sentences.t: ἕλκε δὲ μέσσα λαβών·
sentences.tr: helke de messa labōn·
sentences.l: and he drew them, taking them by the middle;
sentences.i: and taking hold of them in the middle he drew them up;
sentences.n: The subject is still the Father. ἕλκε is the imperfect of ἕλκω ‘draw, pull’ and λαβών the aorist participle of λαμβάνω ‘take’; μέσσα (Attic μέσα) is ‘the middle’, here the middle of the balance, which he holds up to see which pan falls. The half-line ends at a strong stop, and the next unit starts in the middle of this line.

sentences.t:
ῥέπε δ’ Ἕκτορος αἴσιμον ἦμαρ,
ᾤχετο δ’ εἰς Ἀΐδαο, λίπεν δέ ἑ Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων.
sentences.tr:
rhepe d’ Hektoros aisimon ēmar,
ōicheto d’ eis Aïdao, lipen de he Phoibos Apollōn.
sentences.l:
and sank Hector’s fated day,
and it went off to the house of Hades, and left him Phoebus Apollo.
sentences.i: and Hector’s fated day sank, and went off to the house of Hades, and Phoebus Apollo left him.
sentences.n: Hector’s pan is the heavier. ῥέπε is the unaugmented imperfect of ῥέπω ‘sink, incline’, and αἴσιμον ἦμαρ is ‘the fated day’, the day of his death, which is the subject of both ῥέπε and ᾤχετο (the imperfect of οἴχομαι ‘go off’). Ἀΐδαο is the epic genitive of Ἅιδης; the Greek has only ‘into Hades’s’ and ‘house’ is understood. λίπεν is an unaugmented aorist of λείπω, δέ ἑ is ‘and him’, and Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων is the name ‘Phoebus Apollo’, as everywhere. Apollo’s leaving ends the help described at 22.202–204.

sentences.t: Πηλεΐωνα δ’ ἵκανε θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη,
sentences.tr: Pēleïōna d’ hikane thea glaukōpis Athēnē,
sentences.l: And to the son of Peleus came the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena,
sentences.i: The goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, came to the son of Peleus,
sentences.n: The object stands first and the subject last, so Πηλεΐωνα ‘the son of Peleus’ (Achilles) is the one she comes to. ἵκανε is the unaugmented imperfect of ἱκάνω ‘come to’. θεά ‘the goddess’ and γλαυκῶπις ‘gleaming-eyed’ go with Ἀθήνη; the epithet is translated every time the same way. The comma is only a half-stop: the next line says what she did when she arrived.

sentences.t: ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱσταμένη ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr: anchou d’ histamenē epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l: and standing close by, winged words she spoke to him:
sentences.i: Standing close beside him, she spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: This whole line is a formula the poem uses again and again, and its English never changes. ἀγχοῦ ‘close by’ and ἱσταμένη (feminine participle, ‘standing’) tell you where Athena is; ἔπεα πτερόεντα ‘winged words’ is the stock phrase for words that fly from speaker to listener, translated the same way each time. προσηύδα is the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘speak to’. A speech follows at once.

sentences.t:
νῦν δὴ νῶι ἔολπα Διῒ φίλε φαίδιμ’ Ἀχιλλεῦ
οἴσεσθαι μέγα κῦδος Ἀχαιοῖσι προτὶ νῆας
Ἕκτορα δῃώσαντε μάχης ἄατόν περ ἐόντα.
sentences.tr:
nyn dē nōi eolpa Diï phile phaidim’ Achilleu
oisesthai mega kydos Achaioisi proti nēas
Hektora dēiōsante machēs aaton per eonta.
sentences.l:
“Now indeed I expect, we two, dear to Zeus, glorious Achilles,
to bear off great glory for the Achaeans to the ships,
having slain Hector, insatiable of battle though he is.
sentences.i: “Now, I expect, we two, glorious Achilles, dear to Zeus, shall carry off great glory for the Achaeans to the ships, having slain Hector, insatiable of battle though he is.
sentences.n: Athena speaks to Achilles, and says ‘we two’ (νῶι) because she counts herself in. νῶι and the participle δῃώσαντε ‘having slain’ are duals, the Greek number for a pair. ἔολπα is a perfect that means ‘I expect’ (the verb ἔλπομαι). φίλε ‘dear’ (with the dative Διῒ ‘to Zeus’) and φαίδιμ’ Ἀχιλλεῦ ‘glorious Achilles’ are vocatives, and the diaeresis in Διῒ is printed. οἴσεσθαι is the future infinitive of φέρω ‘bear’, Ἀχαιοῖσι the epic dative plural ‘for the Achaeans’, and προτὶ νῆας ‘to the ships’. ἄατον, with μάχης ‘of battle’, is rare, and the usual sense ‘insatiable’ is not certain. ἐόντα is the epic participle of εἰμί, with περ ‘though’.

sentences.t:
οὔ οἱ νῦν ἔτι γ’ ἔστι πεφυγμένον ἄμμε γενέσθαι,
οὐδ’ εἴ κεν μάλα πολλὰ πάθοι ἑκάεργος Ἀπόλλων
προπροκυλινδόμενος πατρὸς Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο.
sentences.tr:
ou hoi nyn eti g’ esti pephygmenon amme genesthai,
oud’ ei ken mala polla pathoi hekaergos Apollōn
proprokylindomenos patros Dios aigiochoio.
sentences.l:
For him now it is no longer possible to have escaped us,
not even if much should suffer far-working Apollo
rolling himself forward before father Zeus, aegis-bearing.
sentences.i: He can no longer escape us now, not even if Apollo, who works from afar, should suffer very much, rolling himself over and over before his father, aegis-bearing Zeus.
sentences.n: οὔ οἱ … ἔστι πεφυγμένον ἄμμε γενέσθαι means ‘it is not possible for him to have escaped us’: ἔστι ‘it is possible’, πεφυγμένον the perfect participle of φεύγω, and ἄμμε the Aeolic accusative for ἡμᾶς ‘us’ (here the two of them). οὐδ’ εἴ κεν … πάθοι ‘not even if he should suffer’ is an optative condition, and πολλά ‘very much’ is adverbial. ἑκάεργος is the epithet of Apollo whose meaning is disputed; the house wording is ‘far-working’ in l and ‘who works from afar’ in i. προπροκυλινδόμενος is ‘rolling himself forward and over’, a picture of someone throwing himself down to plead, before πατρὸς Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο ‘father Zeus, aegis-bearing’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σὺ μὲν νῦν στῆθι καὶ ἄμπνυε, τόνδε δ’ ἐγώ τοι
οἰχομένη πεπιθήσω ἐναντίβιον μαχέσασθαι.
sentences.tr:
alla sy men nyn stēthi kai ampnye, tonde d’ egō toi
oichomenē pepithēsō enantibion machesasthai.
sentences.l:
But you now stand and get your breath, and him, I for you,
going, will persuade to fight head-on.”
sentences.i: But you stand still now and get your breath, and I will go and persuade him to fight you head-on.”
sentences.n: σὺ μὲν … τόνδε δ’ ἐγώ ‘you … but him I’ divides the work: Achilles waits, Athena goes. στῆθι is the aorist imperative of ἵστημι ‘stand’, ἄμπνυε the imperative of ἀναπνέω ‘get your breath back’. τοι ‘for you’ is a dative of the person who gains by it. οἰχομένη ‘going’ is a participle of οἴχομαι, and πεπιθήσω is the reduplicated future of πείθω ‘persuade’. ἐναντίβιον ‘head-on’ is adverbial, with μαχέσασθαι ‘to fight’. Athena’s speech ends here; Hector does not yet know that she is on the field.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτ’ Ἀθηναίη, ὃ δ’ ἐπείθετο, χαῖρε δὲ θυμῷ,
στῆ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπὶ μελίης χαλκογλώχινος ἐρεισθείς.
sentences.tr:
hōs phat’ Athēnaiē, ho d’ epeitheto, chaire de thymōi,
stē d’ ar’ epi meliēs chalkoglōchinos ereistheis.
sentences.l:
So spoke Athena, and he obeyed, and rejoiced in his heart,
and stood leaning on his bronze-pointed ash-spear.
sentences.i: So Athena spoke, and he obeyed and was glad at heart, and he stood leaning on his bronze-pointed ash-spear.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτ’ Ἀθηναίη ‘so spoke Athena’ is a formula that closes a speech; φάτ’ is the unaugmented φάτο, elided, and Ἀθηναίη the epic nominative of Ἀθηναία. ὁ δ’ ἐπείθετο ‘and he obeyed’: ὁ is the article as a pronoun for Achilles, ἐπείθετο the imperfect middle of πείθω ‘obey’. χαῖρε is an unaugmented imperfect, ‘rejoiced’, and θυμῷ is where. στῆ is the aorist ἔστη without augment, ἐρεισθείς the aorist passive participle of ἐρείδω ‘prop, lean’. μελίης is the genitive of μελίη, ‘ash-spear’, and χαλκογλώχινος ‘bronze-pointed’ is from χαλκός ‘bronze’ and γλωχίς ‘point’.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ ἄρα τὸν μὲν ἔλειπε, κιχήσατο δ’ Ἕκτορα δῖον
Δηϊφόβῳ ἐϊκυῖα δέμας καὶ ἀτειρέα φωνήν·
sentences.tr:
hē d’ ara ton men eleipe, kichēsato d’ Hektora dion
Dēïphobōi eïkuia demas kai ateirea phōnēn·
sentences.l:
And she then left him, and came upon heavenly Hector,
like Deiphobus in body and in unwearied voice;
sentences.i: She left him then and came upon heavenly Hector, taking the likeness of Deiphobus in body and in his unwearied voice;
sentences.n: Athena changes shape. ἣ δ’ ἄρα ‘and she then’ is Athena, and the object τὸν μέν ‘him’ is Achilles. ἔλειπε is the imperfect of λείπω, and κιχήσατο the aorist middle of κιχάνω ‘come upon, find’. Δηϊφόβῳ ἐϊκυῖα ‘like Deiphobus’ is a feminine participle (ἐοικυῖα) with a dative, and Deiphobus is a son of Priam, as Hector’s answer will show. δέμας ‘in body’ and ἀτειρέα φωνήν ‘in unwearied voice’ are accusatives of respect: ἀτειρής ‘unwearied’ is ἀ- ‘not’ + τείρω ‘wear down’. δῖος ‘heavenly’ is the stock epithet of Hector as of Achilles.

sentences.t: ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱσταμένη ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr: anchou d’ histamenē epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l: and standing close by, winged words she spoke to him:
sentences.i: Standing close beside him, she spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: The same formula line as before, with the same English: what is said is now Athena’s, in the shape of Deiphobus, to Hector. ἀγχοῦ ‘close by’, ἱσταμένη ‘standing’, ἔπεα πτερόεντα ‘winged words’, προσηύδα ‘she spoke to’. The speech follows at once.

sentences.t:
ἠθεῖ’ ἦ μάλα δή σε βιάζεται ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεὺς
ἄστυ πέρι Πριάμοιο ποσὶν ταχέεσσι διώκων·
sentences.tr:
ēthei’ ē mala dē se biazetai ōkys Achilleus
asty peri Priamoio posin tacheessi diōkōn·
sentences.l:
“Honoured one, truly now swift Achilles presses you hard,
round the town of Priam, pursuing on swift feet;
sentences.i: “My honoured one, swift Achilles is truly pressing you hard, pursuing you on swift feet round the town of Priam;
sentences.n: Athena speaks as Deiphobus, and calls Hector ἠθεῖ’, an elided vocative of ἠθεῖος, a term of address of which the sense is not known; ‘my honoured one’ is the house wording. ἦ μάλα δή is ‘truly, indeed’, and βιάζεται ‘presses hard’ (βιάζομαι, ‘use force on’) has Hector as object. ἄστυ πέρι Πριάμοιο ‘round the town of Priam’ puts πέρι (Attic περί) after its noun; Πριάμοιο has the epic genitive -οιο. ποσὶν ταχέεσσι ‘on swift feet’ is an epic dative plural, and ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς has ὠκύς ‘swift’ as before.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε δὴ στέωμεν καὶ ἀλεξώμεσθα μένοντες.
sentences.tr: all’ age dē steōmen kai alexōmestha menontes.
sentences.l: But come now, let us take our stand and defend ourselves, staying firm.”
sentences.i: But come, let us make a stand and defend ourselves by holding our ground.”
sentences.n: A whole line the poem has used before, with the same English. ἀλλ’ ἄγε δή ‘but come now’ introduces the proposal. στέωμεν and ἀλεξώμεσθα are subjunctives of exhortation, ‘let us’; στέωμεν is the epic uncontracted form of στῶμεν, from ἵστημι ‘stand’. μένοντες ‘staying firm’ is a present participle and says how they will defend themselves. The false Deiphobus’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε μέγας κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ aute proseeipe megas korythaiolos Hektōr·
sentences.l: Her then in turn addressed great Hector of the glancing helmet:
sentences.i: Then great Hector of the glancing helmet spoke to her in turn:
sentences.n: A whole speech-introduction line, with the same English each time it recurs. τήν is the article as a pronoun, ‘her’: the Greek says ‘her’, because the poet knows it is Athena, though Hector sees only Deiphobus. αὖτε ‘in turn’; προσέειπε ‘addressed’ is the epic aorist of προσεῖπον. κορυθαίολος, ‘of the glancing helmet’ (κόρυς ‘helmet’ + αἰόλος ‘quick-moving, glancing’), is the stock epithet of Hector, with μέγας ‘great’.

sentences.t:
Δηΐφοβ’ ἦ μέν μοι τὸ πάρος πολὺ φίλτατος ἦσθα
γνωτῶν οὓς Ἑκάβη ἠδὲ Πρίαμος τέκε παῖδας·
sentences.tr:
Dēïphob’ ē men moi to paros poly philtatos ēstha
gnōtōn hous Hekabē ēde Priamos teke paidas·
sentences.l:
“Deiphobus, truly before this by far the dearest you were to me
of the kinsfolk, the children whom Hecuba and Priam bore;
sentences.i: “Deiphobus, you were by far the dearest to me, before now, of all my kinsfolk, the children whom Hecuba and Priam bore;
sentences.n: Hector speaks to the false Deiphobus. Δηΐφοβ’ is an elided vocative, with the diaeresis printed. ἦ μέν ‘truly’; τὸ πάρος is the article as an adverb, ‘before now’; φίλτατος is the superlative ‘dearest’, ἦσθα the second person of εἰμί. γνωτῶν is the genitive plural of γνωτός ‘kinsman’; in the house wording it is ‘kinsfolk’, and here it means brothers and sisters, the children of one pair of parents. τέκε is the unaugmented aorist of τίκτω ‘bear’, with Ἑκάβη ‘Hecuba’ and Πρίαμος ‘Priam’.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ἔτι καὶ μᾶλλον νοέω φρεσὶ τιμήσασθαι,
ὃς ἔτλης ἐμεῦ εἵνεκ’, ἐπεὶ ἴδες ὀφθαλμοῖσι,
τείχεος ἐξελθεῖν, ἄλλοι δ’ ἔντοσθε μένουσι.
sentences.tr:
nyn d’ eti kai mallon noeō phresi timēsasthai,
hos etlēs emeu heinek’, epei ides ophthalmoisi,
teicheos exelthein, alloi d’ entosthe menousi.
sentences.l:
but now even more I intend in my mind to honour you,
you who dared, for my sake, since you saw with your eyes,
to come out of the wall, while the others stay inside.”
sentences.i: but now I am minded to honour you in my heart even more, you who dared to come out of the wall for my sake, since you saw it with your own eyes, while the others stay inside.”
sentences.n: νοέω φρεσί … τιμήσασθαι is ‘I intend in my mind to honour’, with the aorist middle infinitive of τιμάω. ὃς ἔτλης ‘you who dared’ has ὅς as a relative and ἔτλης as the aorist of τλάω ‘endure, dare’. ἐμεῦ εἵνεκ’ is ‘for my sake’ (ἐμεῦ is the epic genitive, εἵνεκα Attic ἕνεκα). ἴδες is an unaugmented aorist, and ὀφθαλμοῖσι an epic dative plural; the Greek does not say what Deiphobus saw, and the free English adds ‘it’. τείχεος is the epic genitive of τεῖχος ‘wall’, and ἔντοσθε ‘inside’ is an adverb.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe thea glaukōpis Athēnē·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena:
sentences.i: Then the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: A whole speech-introduction line, the same every time it comes. τόν is ‘him’, Hector; αὖτε ‘in turn’, προσέειπε ‘addressed’. θεά ‘goddess’ and γλαυκῶπις ‘gleaming-eyed’ go with the name; the poet says the goddess although Hector sees Deiphobus. Athena answers, and goes on playing the part.

sentences.t:
ἠθεῖ’ ἦ μὲν πολλὰ πατὴρ καὶ πότνια μήτηρ
λίσσονθ’ ἑξείης γουνούμενοι, ἀμφὶ δ’ ἑταῖροι,
αὖθι μένειν· τοῖον γὰρ ὑποτρομέουσιν ἅπαντες·
sentences.tr:
ēthei’ ē men polla patēr kai potnia mētēr
lissonth’ hexeiēs gounoumenoi, amphi d’ hetairoi,
authi menein· toion gar hypotromeousin hapantes·
sentences.i: “My honoured one, our father and our lady mother begged me again and again, in order, clasping my knees, and my companions all round, to stay there; for they all tremble so before him;
sentences.n: Athena goes on as Deiphobus. ἠθεῖ’ is the same term of address as before, sense not known. The verb is λίσσονθ’, an elided imperfect of λίσσομαι ‘beg’ without augment, and its subjects are ‘father and lady mother’ (the Greek has no ‘our’ or ‘me’; the sense supplies them). ἑξείης is ‘in order’, and γουνούμενοι is from γουνόομαι ‘clasp the knees’, the gesture of a suppliant; ἀμφὶ δ’ ἑταῖροι ‘and round about, the companions’ borrows the verb. αὖθι is ‘there, on the spot’. τοῖον is either ‘such a man’ or ‘so’; the Greek is compressed. ὑποτρομέουσιν is ‘tremble before’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἐμὸς ἔνδοθι θυμὸς ἐτείρετο πένθεϊ λυγρῷ.
sentences.tr: all’ emos endothi thymos eteireto pentheï lygrōi.
sentences.l: but my own heart within was being worn down with grievous grief.
sentences.i: but my own heart within me was being worn down by grievous grief.
sentences.n: ἀλλά ‘but’ turns away from the parents’ plea. ἐμός ‘my own’ is a possessive adjective, emphatic; θυμός is ‘heart’, and ἔνδοθι ‘within’ an adverb. ἐτείρετο is the imperfect passive of τείρω ‘wear down’. πένθεϊ λυγρῷ ‘with grievous grief’ is a dative, with the diaeresis printed in πένθεϊ; λυγρός ‘grievous’. The line says why the false Deiphobus came out: it was grief for Hector.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ἰθὺς μεμαῶτε μαχώμεθα, μὴ δέ τι δούρων
ἔστω φειδωλή, ἵνα εἴδομεν εἴ κεν Ἀχιλλεὺς
νῶϊ κατακτείνας ἔναρα βροτόεντα φέρηται
νῆας ἔπι γλαφυράς, ἦ κεν σῷ δουρὶ δαμήῃ.
sentences.tr:
nyn d’ ithys memaōte machōmetha, mē de ti dourōn
estō pheidōlē, hina eidomen ei ken Achilleus
nōï katakteinas enara brotoenta pherētai
nēas epi glaphyras, ē ken sōi douri damēēi.
sentences.l:
But now straight at him, eager, let us fight, and let there be no
sparing of spears, so that we may know whether Achilles,
having killed us two, will carry off bloody spoils
to the hollow ships, or by your spear will be overcome.”
sentences.i: But now let us two fight straight at him, with all our eagerness, and let there be no sparing of spears, so that we may learn whether Achilles will kill us both and carry off our bloody spoils to the hollow ships, or be overcome by your spear.”
sentences.n: The proposal is one long sentence. ἰθύς ‘straight at him’ is an adverb (Achilles is understood), and μεμαῶτε is the dual perfect participle of μέμαα ‘be eager’, ‘we two eager’. μαχώμεθα is a subjunctive of exhortation. μὴ δέ τι is μηδέ τι; ἔστω is ‘let there be’, with φειδωλή ‘sparing’ and δούρων, genitive plural of δόρυ ‘spear’. ἵνα εἴδομεν is the subjunctive of οἶδα; εἰ κεν … φέρηται ‘whether he will carry off’. κατακτείνας is the aorist participle ‘having killed’, νῶϊ the dual (‘us two’, the object), ἔναρα βροτόεντα ‘bloody spoils’, and νῆας ἔπι γλαφυράς ‘to the hollow ships’ puts ἐπί after its noun. δαμήῃ is the aorist passive subjunctive of δαμάζω.

sentences.t: ὣς φαμένη καὶ κερδοσύνῃ ἡγήσατ’ Ἀθήνη·
sentences.tr: hōs phamenē kai kerdosynēi hēgēsat’ Athēnē·
sentences.l: So saying, and with cunning, led the way Athena;
sentences.i: So speaking, Athena led the way with her cunning;
sentences.n: ὣς φαμένη ‘so saying’ is the participle of φημί, and ἡγήσατ’ is the aorist of ἡγέομαι ‘lead the way’, with its ending elided. κερδοσύνῃ is a dative of means, ‘with cunning’, from κέρδος ‘gain’ (and so also ‘shrewd profit’); the καί ties it to the participle. ἡγήσατ’ has no object: she goes first and Hector follows, thinking his brother is beside him.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὅτε δὴ σχεδὸν ἦσαν ἐπ’ ἀλλήλοισιν ἰόντες,
τὸν πρότερος προσέειπε μέγας κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ hote dē schedon ēsan ep’ allēloisin iontes,
ton proteros proseeipe megas korythaiolos Hektōr·
sentences.l:
And when they were near, going against one another,
him first addressed great Hector of the glancing helmet:
sentences.i: And when they were near, advancing on one another, great Hector of the glancing helmet spoke to him first:
sentences.n: The first line repeats a line of the poem, and its English is carried over. οἳ δ’ ὅτε δή ‘and when’ the pair, Hector and Achilles; ἦσαν is the imperfect of εἰμί, and ἰόντες the participle of εἶμι ‘go’. τόν is ‘him’, Achilles, and πρότερος ‘first’ says that Hector speaks before Achilles does. προσέειπε ‘addressed’; κορυθαίολος ‘of the glancing helmet’ is the stock epithet. The speech follows.

sentences.t:
οὔ σ’ ἔτι Πηλέος υἱὲ φοβήσομαι, ὡς τὸ πάρος περ
τρὶς περὶ ἄστυ μέγα Πριάμου δίον, οὐδέ ποτ’ ἔτλην
μεῖναι ἐπερχόμενον·
sentences.tr:
ou s’ eti Pēleos huie phobēsomai, hōs to paros per
tris peri asty mega Priamou dion, oude pot’ etlēn
meinai eperchomenon·
sentences.i: “I shall no longer be afraid of you, son of Peleus, as I was before, when three times I fled round the great town of Priam, and never dared to wait for you as you came on;
sentences.n: οὔ σ’ ἔτι φοβήσομαι is ‘I shall no longer fear you’: φοβήσομαι is the future middle of φοβέομαι, which takes the person feared as its object. Πηλέος υἱέ is a vocative, with the Ionic genitive Πηλέος (Attic Πηλέως). ὡς τὸ πάρος περ is ‘as before indeed’, and the picture is the three laps: τρὶς … δίον, with δίον ‘I fled’ the unaugmented imperfect of δίω ‘flee in fear’, a different verb from δίεμαι ‘chase’ (δίηται at 22.189), and not a form of διώκω. οὐδέ ποτ’ ἔτλην ‘and never dared’ takes the aorist infinitive μεῖναι ‘to wait for’, and ἐπερχόμενον is the participle ‘as you came on’ in the accusative, agreeing with the σε that is understood.

sentences.t:
νῦν αὖτέ με θυμὸς ἀνῆκε
στήμεναι ἀντία σεῖο·
sentences.tr:
nyn aute me thymos anēke
stēmenai antia seio·
sentences.l:
now again my heart has driven me
to stand against you;
sentences.i: but now my heart has moved me, in my turn, to stand and face you;
sentences.n: νῦν αὖτε is ‘now again’, and ‘in my turn’ says the same: Hector, who ran, now stands. ἀνῆκε is the aorist of ἀνίημι ‘send up, impel’, with θυμός ‘heart’ as subject and με as object. στήμεναι is the epic infinitive of ἵστημι (Attic στῆναι), ἀντία ‘against, opposite’ an adverb, and σεῖο the epic genitive of σύ.

sentences.t: ἕλοιμί κεν ἤ κεν ἁλοίην.
sentences.tr: heloimi ken ē ken haloiēn.
sentences.l: I might take, or I might be taken.
sentences.i: Either I may kill you, or I may be killed.
sentences.n: ἕλοιμι κεν ἤ κεν ἁλοίην has two optatives with κεν, each a possibility: ἕλοιμι is the aorist of αἱρέω ‘take’, and ἁλοίην the aorist optative of ἁλίσκομαι ‘be taken’, which serves as the passive of αἱρέω and comes from the same root. In fighting ‘take’ means ‘take down’, ‘kill’; no object is stated, and σε is understood. The two halves are joined by ἤ ‘or’, the one active in form, the other passive in sense.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε δεῦρο θεοὺς ἐπιδώμεθα·
sentences.tr: all’ age deuro theous epidōmetha·
sentences.l: But come, here, let us call in the gods;
sentences.i: But come, let us call on the gods as witnesses;
sentences.n: Hector now proposes a pledge before the fight. ἀλλ’ ἄγε is ‘but come’, and δεῦρο ‘here’. ἐπιδώμεθα is an aorist subjunctive of exhortation of the middle of ἐπιδίδωμι, which means something like ‘give over, make one’s own’; the sense is not certain, and the usual reading, ‘call in the gods as witnesses’, is taken because the next line gives that as the reason. θεούς is the object.

sentences.t:
τοὶ γὰρ ἄριστοι
μάρτυροι ἔσσονται καὶ ἐπίσκοποι ἁρμονιάων·
sentences.tr:
toi gar aristoi
martyroi essontai kai episkopoi harmoniaōn·
sentences.l:
for they are the best
witnesses and guardians of compacts;
sentences.i: for they will be the best witnesses and guardians of our compacts;
sentences.n: τοὶ γάρ is printed as two words: τοί is the article as a pronoun, ‘they’ (the gods). ἄριστοι is ‘best’, μάρτυροι the epic nominative plural of μάρτυς ‘witness’, and ἔσσονται the epic future of εἰμί ‘will be’. ἐπίσκοποι are those who look over (the word is ‘scout’ at 10.38, where a man is sent to watch the enemy): ‘guardians’ is chosen because it is the gods who would watch over the compact. ἁρμονιάων is the epic genitive plural of ἁρμονία, a rare noun from ἁρμόζω ‘fit together’, here ‘compact’.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἐγώ σ’ ἔκπαγλον ἀεικιῶ, αἴ κεν ἐμοὶ Ζεὺς
δώῃ καμμονίην, σὴν δὲ ψυχὴν ἀφέλωμαι·
sentences.tr:
ou gar egō s’ ekpaglon aeikiō, ai ken emoi Zeus
dōēi kammoniēn, sēn de psychēn aphelōmai·
sentences.l:
For I shall not treat you terribly unseemly, if to me Zeus
gives staying-power and I take away your soul;
sentences.i: For I shall not abuse you terribly, if Zeus grants me endurance and I take your life;
sentences.n: Hector now says what he will do if he wins. ἀεικιῶ is the future of ἀεικίζω ‘treat unseemly, abuse’, and ἔκπαγλον is the adverb ‘terribly’. αἴ κεν is εἰ ἄν ‘if’, δώῃ the aorist subjunctive of δίδωμι ‘give’ (Attic δῷ), and Ζεύς comes at the end of the first line. καμμονίη is a rare word, probably ‘staying-power, holding out’, and its exact sense is not certain. ἀφέλωμαι is the aorist subjunctive middle of ἀφαιρέομαι ‘take away’, with σὴν ψυχήν ‘your soul’ as object; ‘your life’ in the free English is the idiom for the same thing.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐπεὶ ἄρ κέ σε συλήσω κλυτὰ τεύχε’ Ἀχιλλεῦ
νεκρὸν Ἀχαιοῖσιν δώσω πάλιν·
sentences.tr:
all’ epei ar ke se sylēsō klyta teuche’ Achilleu
nekron Achaioisin dōsō palin·
sentences.l:
but when I have stripped you of your famous armour, Achilles,
the corpse I will give back to the Achaeans;
sentences.i: But when I have stripped you of your famous armour, Achilles, I will give your body back to the Achaeans;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἐπεὶ ἄρ κε … συλήσω has κε with an aorist subjunctive, ‘when I have stripped’; συλάω is ‘strip a slain man of his arms’. κλυτὰ τεύχε’ is ‘famous armour’ (τεύχεα elided), Ἀχιλλεῦ a vocative. δώσω is the future of δίδωμι, νεκρόν ‘corpse’ the object, Ἀχαιοῖσιν the epic dative plural, and πάλιν ‘back’. The offer is what Hector asks Achilles for in return.

sentences.t: ὣς δὲ σὺ ῥέζειν.
sentences.tr: hōs de sy rhezein.
sentences.l: and you, so to do.”
sentences.i: and you must do the same.”
sentences.n: ὣς δὲ σὺ ῥέζειν is a half-line with no finite verb: ῥέζειν ‘to do’ is an infinitive used as an imperative, which Homer often uses for a command, ‘and you do so’. ὥς ‘so, thus’ points back to what Hector has just promised. Hector’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπόδρα ἰδὼν προσέφη πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ar’ hypodra idōn prosephē podas ōkys Achilleus·
sentences.l: Him then with a scowl looking addressed swift-in-feet Achilles:
sentences.i: Then Achilles, swift of foot, looking at him with a scowl, spoke to him:
sentences.n: A whole line the poem has used before, with the same English. τὸν δ’ ἄρ’ ‘and him then’ is Hector. ὑπόδρα ἰδών is ‘looking with a scowl’: ὑπόδρα is an adverb made from ὑπό ‘under’ and a verb of looking, the glare from under the brows, and ἰδών is the aorist participle of ὁράω. προσέφη is the unaugmented aorist ‘addressed’. πόδας ὠκύς ‘swift of foot’ is the stock epithet of Achilles, a noun and adjective with the accusative of respect, translated every time.

sentences.t: Ἕκτορ μή μοι ἄλαστε συνημοσύνας ἀγόρευε·
sentences.tr: Hektor mē moi alaste synēmosynas agoreue·
sentences.l: “Hector, unforgettable one, do not speak terms to me;
sentences.i: “Hector, you whom I cannot forget, do not speak to me of terms;
sentences.n: Achilles answers, and refuses. μή … ἀγόρευε is a prohibition, ‘do not speak’, with the present imperative. ἄλαστε is a vocative of ἄλαστος, which seems to be ‘not to be forgotten’ (ἀ- + λανθάνω), and which is used as an insult; its exact sense is disputed, and the house wording keeps the plain reading. συνημοσύνας is the accusative plural of συνημοσύνη, a rare noun for a mutual agreement, here ‘terms’.

sentences.t:
ὡς οὐκ ἔστι λέουσι καὶ ἀνδράσιν ὅρκια πιστά,
οὐδὲ λύκοι τε καὶ ἄρνες ὁμόφρονα θυμὸν ἔχουσιν,
ἀλλὰ κακὰ φρονέουσι διαμπερὲς ἀλλήλοισιν,
sentences.tr:
hōs ouk esti leousi kai andrasin horkia pista,
oude lykoi te kai arnes homophrona thymon echousin,
alla kaka phroneousi diamperes allēloisin,
sentences.l:
as there are not for lions and men faithful oaths,
nor do wolves and lambs have a like-minded heart,
but evil they think continuously toward one another,
sentences.i: As there are no faithful oaths between lions and men, and wolves and lambs have no common mind, but think ill of one another without a break,
sentences.n: The comparison has two halves; its application, introduced by ὣς, follows in the next unit. ὡς οὐκ ἔστι is ‘as there is not’; λέουσι is the epic dative plural of λέων ‘lion’; ὅρκια πιστά is ‘faithful oaths’, with the house rendering of πιστός. λύκοι τε καὶ ἄρνες ‘wolves and lambs’ is the pair of natural enemies. ὁμόφρονα θυμόν is ‘a like-minded heart’. κακὰ φρονέουσι is ‘they think evil’ (uncontracted), διαμπερές ‘continuously’ an adverb, and ἀλλήλοισιν ‘toward one another’ an epic dative plural.

sentences.t:
ὣς οὐκ ἔστ’ ἐμὲ καὶ σὲ φιλήμεναι, οὐδέ τι νῶϊν
ὅρκια ἔσσονται, πρίν γ’ ἢ ἕτερόν γε πεσόντα
αἵματος ἆσαι Ἄρηα ταλαύρινον πολεμιστήν.
sentences.tr:
hōs ouk est’ eme kai se philēmenai, oude ti nōïn
horkia essontai, prin g’ ē heteron ge pesonta
haimatos asai Arēa talaurinon polemistēn.
sentences.l:
so it is not possible for me and you to be friends, nor for us two
oaths will there be, before at least one, having fallen,
has glutted with blood Ares, the shield-enduring warrior.
sentences.i: so there can be no friendship between you and me, nor will there be oaths between us two, until one or the other has fallen and glutted Ares, the warrior who bears the hide shield, with his blood.
sentences.n: ὣς answers ὡς in the unit before: ‘as … so’. οὐκ ἔστ’ ἐμὲ καὶ σὲ φιλήμεναι is ‘it is not possible for me and you to be friends’, with ἔστ’ elided and φιλήμεναι the epic infinitive of φιλέω; νῶϊν is the dual, ‘us two’, with the diaeresis printed. πρίν γ’ ἢ is ‘before, until’, and ἕτερόν γε πεσόντα ‘one of the two at least, having fallen’. αἵματος ἆσαι Ἄρηα ‘to glut Ares with blood’ makes Ares the war-god, and ἆσαι is the aorist infinitive of ἄω ‘sate’. ταλαύρινον ‘shield-enduring’ (τλῆναι ‘endure’ + ῥινός ‘hide’, the traditional sense) and πολεμιστήν ‘warrior’ go with Ares. This last line has been used before.

sentences.t: παντοίης ἀρετῆς μιμνήσκεο·
sentences.tr: pantoiēs aretēs mimnēskeo·
sentences.l: Of every kind of excellence be mindful;
sentences.i: Call to mind every kind of excellence;
sentences.n: παντοίης ἀρετῆς is a genitive, because μιμνήσκεο, the imperative of μιμνήσκομαι ‘remember, be mindful of’, takes the genitive. ἀρετή is ‘excellence’, here excellence at fighting, in the sense that Achilles is telling him to use all he has. The line is bitter: Achilles has just said there is no bargain.

sentences.t:
νῦν σε μάλα χρὴ
αἰχμητήν τ’ ἔμεναι καὶ θαρσαλέον πολεμιστήν.
sentences.tr:
nyn se mala chrē
aichmētēn t’ emenai kai tharsaleon polemistēn.
sentences.l:
now you very much must
be a spearman and a bold warrior.
sentences.i: now, above all, you must be a spearman and a bold warrior.
sentences.n: νῦν σε μάλα χρή is ‘now you very much must’: χρή ‘it is necessary’ takes the accusative σε and the infinitive ἔμεναι, the epic form of εἶναι ‘to be’. αἰχμητήν is ‘spearman’, θαρσαλέον ‘bold’, and πολεμιστήν ‘warrior’. The second line is a line the poem has used before; there the same words were said in praise of Hector, and here Achilles turns them on him as a challenge.

sentences.t:
οὔ τοι ἔτ’ ἔσθ’ ὑπάλυξις, ἄφαρ δέ σε Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη
ἔγχει ἐμῷ δαμάᾳ·
sentences.tr:
ou toi et’ esth’ hypalyxis, aphar de se Pallas Athēnē
enchei emōi damaāi·
sentences.l:
No longer for you is there escape; at once Pallas Athena
will subdue you by my spear;
sentences.i: You have no way of escape any more: in a moment Pallas Athena will overcome you by my spear;
sentences.n: οὔ τοι ἔτ’ ἔσθ’ ὑπάλυξις is ‘there is no longer for you any escape’: τοι ‘for you’, ἔσθ’ for ἔστι, and ὑπάλυξις a noun from ὑπαλύσκω, ‘getting out from under’. ἄφαρ ‘at once’; Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη is ‘Pallas Athena’. δαμάᾳ is an epic future of δαμάζω ‘subdue’, with ἔγχει ἐμῷ ‘by my spear’ as the means; Achilles thinks of Athena as helping his spear. The line ends with a strong stop in the middle of the verse.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ἀθρόα πάντ’ ἀποτίσεις
κήδε’ ἐμῶν ἑτάρων οὓς ἔκτανες ἔγχεϊ θύων.
sentences.tr:
nyn d’ athroa pant’ apotiseis
kēde’ emōn hetarōn hous ektanes encheï thyōn.
sentences.l:
and now all together you will pay for all
the sorrows of my companions whom you killed with your spear, raging.”
sentences.i: and now you will pay for all the sorrows of my companions together, those you killed, raging with your spear.”
sentences.n: νῦν δ’ ἀθρόα πάντ’ ἀποτίσεις is ‘and now all together you will pay for all’: ἀθρόα is ‘together’, neuter plural, and the future of ἀποτίνω ‘pay back’ takes the sorrows as its object. κήδε’ is κήδεα ‘sorrows’, elided. ἐμῶν ἑτάρων is the genitive plural of ἕταρος, the epic form of ἑταῖρος ‘companion’. ἔκτανες is the aorist of κτείνω ‘kill’, and ἔγχεϊ is the dative with the diaeresis printed. θύων is a participle of θύω ‘rage’. Achilles’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: ἦ ῥα, καὶ ἀμπεπαλὼν προΐει δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος·
sentences.tr: ē rha, kai ampepalōn proïei dolichoskion enchos·
sentences.l: He spoke, and having brandished it he sent forth his long-shadowed spear;
sentences.i: So he said, and brandishing it he sent forth his long-shadowed spear;
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα is ‘he spoke’, the short ἦ that closes a speech and starts the action. ἀμπεπαλών is the reduplicated aorist participle of ἀναπάλλω ‘swing up, brandish’, and προΐει the imperfect of προΐημι ‘send forth’. δολιχόσκιον ‘long-shadowed’ (δολιχός ‘long’ + σκιά ‘shadow’) is the stock epithet of ἔγχος ‘spear’ and is translated every time. This line is a line the poem has used before; there it continued with the throw, here it ends at a strong stop.

sentences.t: καὶ τὸ μὲν ἄντα ἰδὼν ἠλεύατο φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ·
sentences.tr: kai to men anta idōn ēleuato phaidimos Hektōr·
sentences.l: and that one, indeed, looking straight at it, avoided, glorious Hector;
sentences.i: and glorious Hector saw it coming straight at him and avoided it;
sentences.n: τὸ μέν is ‘that one’, the spear, set against τὸ δέ in the next unit. ἄντα ἰδών is ‘looking straight at it’, and ἠλεύατο the aorist of ἀλέομαι ‘avoid’. φαίδιμος ‘glorious’ is the stock epithet of Hector. The object comes first and the subject last, as often in this part.

sentences.t:
ἕζετο γὰρ προϊδών, τὸ δ’ ὑπέρπτατο χάλκεον ἔγχος,
ἐν γαίῃ δ’ ἐπάγη·
sentences.tr:
hezeto gar proïdōn, to d’ hyperptato chalkeon enchos,
en gaiēi d’ epagē·
sentences.l:
for he sat down, seeing it beforehand, and it flew over, the bronze spear,
and in the earth it stuck;
sentences.i: for he crouched, having seen it beforehand, and the bronze spear flew over him and stuck in the earth;
sentences.n: ἕζετο is the unaugmented imperfect of ἕζομαι ‘sit down’, and here means that he ducked low. προϊδών is the aorist participle ‘having seen beforehand’. ὑπέρπτατο is the aorist of ὑπερπέτομαι ‘fly over’, unaugmented, and χάλκεον ἔγχος ‘the bronze spear’ is its subject. ἐν γαίῃ is ‘in the earth’ (γαίη is the epic form of γῆ), and ἐπάγη is the aorist passive of πήγνυμι ‘fix’. The half-line ends at a strong stop.

sentences.t:
ἀνὰ δ’ ἥρπασε Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη,
ἂψ δ’ Ἀχιλῆϊ δίδου, λάθε δ’ Ἕκτορα ποιμένα λαῶν.
sentences.tr:
ana d’ hērpase Pallas Athēnē,
aps d’ Achilēï didou, lathe d’ Hektora poimena laōn.
sentences.l:
and up she snatched it, Pallas Athena,
and back to Achilles gave it, and escaped the notice of Hector, shepherd of the people.
sentences.i: and Pallas Athena snatched it up and gave it back to Achilles, without Hector, shepherd of the people, noticing.
sentences.n: ἀνὰ … ἥρπασε is tmesis of ἀναρπάζω ‘snatch up’, with the subject Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη; ἥρπασε is the aorist. ἂψ ‘back’, and δίδου is the imperfect of δίδωμι, ‘gave’ (literally ‘was giving’). Ἀχιλῆϊ is the epic dative, with a single λ. λάθε is the unaugmented aorist of λανθάνω, taking the accusative as at the start of the part, ‘she escaped the notice of’. ποιμένα λαῶν ‘shepherd of the people’ is the stock epithet of Hector in apposition, translated every time.

sentences.t: Ἕκτωρ δὲ προσέειπεν ἀμύμονα Πηλεΐωνα·
sentences.tr: Hektōr de proseeipen amymona Pēleïōna·
sentences.l: And Hector addressed the blameless son of Peleus:
sentences.i: Then Hector spoke to the blameless son of Peleus:
sentences.n: ἀμύμονα ‘blameless’ is the stock epithet of Achilles here, translated the same way each time. προσέειπεν is the epic aorist of προσεῖπον with movable ν, ‘addressed’. Πηλεΐωνα ‘son of Peleus’ is the patronymic. A speech follows.

sentences.t:
ἤμβροτες, οὐδ’ ἄρα πώ τι θεοῖς ἐπιείκελ’ Ἀχιλλεῦ
ἐκ Διὸς ἠείδης τὸν ἐμὸν μόρον, ἦ τοι ἔφης γε·
sentences.tr:
ēmbrotes, oud’ ara pō ti theois epieikel’ Achilleu
ek Dios ēeidēs ton emon moron, ē toi ephēs ge·
sentences.l:
“You missed, and not at all yet, it seems, resembling the gods, Achilles,
from Zeus had you known my doom, though you said so indeed;
sentences.i: “You missed, Achilles, you who are like the gods; you had not known my doom from Zeus after all, though you did say so;
sentences.n: Hector speaks to Achilles after the miss. ἤμβροτες is the aorist of ἁμαρτάνω ‘miss’. οὐδ’ ἄρα πώ τι is ‘not yet at all, it seems’; ἄρα marks that he has found something out. θεοῖς ἐπιείκελ’ Ἀχιλλεῦ is the vocative ‘resembling the gods, Achilles’. ἐκ Διός is ‘from Zeus’ as the source of knowledge, and ἠείδης is the lengthened Homeric form of the past of οἶδα, ‘you knew’. τὸν ἐμὸν μόρον is ‘my doom’. ἦ τοι ἔφης γε ‘though you indeed said so’ points to Achilles’ claim that Athena will kill him.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά τις ἀρτιεπὴς καὶ ἐπίκλοπος ἔπλεο μύθων,
ὄφρά σ’ ὑποδείσας μένεος ἀλκῆς τε λάθωμαι.
sentences.tr:
alla tis artiepēs kai epiklopos epleo mythōn,
ophra s’ hypodeisas meneos alkēs te lathōmai.
sentences.l:
but a glib one and a trickster in words you have turned out to be,
so that, fearing you, I might forget fury and might.
sentences.i: No, you have turned out a glib talker, a trickster in words, so that I should fear you and forget my fury and my might.
sentences.n: ἀλλά ‘but’ gives Hector’s guess: that Achilles’ words were meant to frighten him. τις ἀρτιεπής is ‘someone glib’, and ἀρτιεπής is traditionally ‘ready of speech’ (ἄρτιος ‘fitting’ + ἔπος ‘word’). ἐπίκλοπος μύθων is ‘a trickster in words’, and ἔπλεο ‘you have turned out’. ὄφρα with the subjunctive gives the aim, and ὑποδείσας is the aorist participle ‘having feared’, so ‘fearing you’. λάθωμαι is a subjunctive middle of λανθάνομαι, ‘forget’, which takes the genitive (μένεος ἀλκῆς τε), whereas the active in the earlier lines took the accusative of the person who notices.

sentences.t:
οὐ μέν μοι φεύγοντι μεταφρένῳ ἐν δόρυ πήξεις,
ἀλλ’ ἰθὺς μεμαῶτι διὰ στήθεσφιν ἔλασσον
εἴ τοι ἔδωκε θεός·
sentences.tr:
ou men moi pheugonti metaphrenōi en dory pēxeis,
all’ ithys memaōti dia stēthesphin elasson
ei toi edōke theos·
sentences.i: You will not plant your spear in my back as I run away; as I charge straight at you, drive it through my chest, if a god has granted you that;
sentences.n: οὐ μέν μοι φεύγοντι … πήξεις is ‘you will not fix in me as I flee’: φεύγοντι is a dative participle, and ἐν … πήξεις (tmesis) the future of πήγνυμι ‘fix’ with μεταφρένῳ ‘in the back’. ἀλλ’ ἰθὺς μεμαῶτι is ‘but to me, eager, straight on’: ἰθύς ‘straight on’ is an adverb, and μεμαῶτι, again a dative participle, agrees with μοι. διὰ στήθεσφιν is ‘through the chest’ with -φιν, an old ending that stands for a plain case. ἔλασσον is the aorist imperative of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’. εἴ τοι ἔδωκε θεός is ‘if a god has given you’, and the Greek does not say what; ‘that’ is supplied.

sentences.t:
νῦν αὖτ’ ἐμὸν ἔγχος ἄλευαι
χάλκεον·
sentences.tr:
nyn aut’ emon enchos aleuai
chalkeon·
sentences.l:
now in your turn my spear avoid,
the bronze one;
sentences.i: Now it is your turn to avoid my bronze spear;
sentences.n: νῦν αὖτε is ‘now again, in your turn’. ἄλευαι is the aorist imperative middle of ἀλέομαι ‘avoid’, the verb used of Hector at ἠλεύατο above. ἄλευαι ends the line, and χάλκεον ‘bronze’, which belongs with ἔγχος ‘spear’, stands first in the next, held over the line-end for emphasis.

sentences.t: ὡς δή μιν σῷ ἐν χροῒ πᾶν κομίσαιο.
sentences.tr: hōs dē min sōi en chroï pan komisaio.
sentences.l: Thus indeed it, all of it, in your flesh may you receive.
sentences.i: May you take the whole of it into your own flesh!
sentences.n: ὡς δή with an optative is a wish. κομίσαιο is the aorist optative middle of κομίζω, here ‘receive, take to oneself’, with μιν ‘it’ (the spear) as object and πᾶν ‘all of it’ in apposition. σῷ ἐν χροῒ is ‘in your flesh’, with the diaeresis printed in χροῒ. The wish is a curse.

sentences.t:
καί κεν ἐλαφρότερος πόλεμος Τρώεσσι γένοιτο
σεῖο καταφθιμένοιο·
sentences.tr:
kai ken elaphroteros polemos Trōessi genoito
seio kataphthimenoio·
sentences.l:
And lighter would the war become for the Trojans,
you having perished;
sentences.i: And the war would be lighter for the Trojans if you were dead;
sentences.n: καί κεν … γένοιτο is a potential optative, ‘would become’. ἐλαφρότερος is the comparative of ἐλαφρός ‘light’, πόλεμος the subject, and Τρώεσσι the epic dative plural ‘for the Trojans’. σεῖο καταφθιμένοιο is a genitive absolute, ‘you having perished’: σεῖο is the epic genitive of σύ, and καταφθιμένοιο the aorist middle participle of καταφθίνω. The unit ends at a strong stop in the middle of the line.

sentences.t: σὺ γάρ σφισι πῆμα μέγιστον.
sentences.tr: sy gar sphisi pēma megiston.
sentences.l: for you are to them the greatest woe.”
sentences.i: for you are their greatest woe.”
sentences.n: σὺ γάρ σφισι πῆμα μέγιστον has no verb; ἐστί ‘are’ is understood. σφισι is the epic dative of the third-person plural, ‘to them’, and πῆμα ‘woe’ keeps the house wording; μέγιστον is the superlative ‘greatest’. Hector’s speech ends here, and with it the part.
